newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health fraud prosecutions rising.
newsitem.headline: U.S. health fraud prosecutions rising.

text.p: The Justice Department on Wednesday reported increased successes in combating the "crime of the 90s" -- health care fraud that is believed to cost tens of billions of dollars a year.

Whether committed by laboratories, home care companies, doctors or hospitals, outright fraud as well as waste and abuse may account for as much as 10 percent of all U.S. health care spending, or $100 billion a year, according to a General Accounting Office report.
The federal government spends billions of dollars a year on Medicare, Medicaid, veterans' and other health programs.
Over the past two years, U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno has directed more resources at the health fraud, and the number of criminal and civil investigations have soared.
According to a Justice Department report released Monday, the number of Federal Bureau of Investigation health-related investigations tripled between 1992 and 1996, to 2,200 cases.
Criminal prosecutions increased from 83 cases to 246 cases, many with multiple defendants, and convictions rose from 90 defendants to 307.
Civil health fraud cases rose even more dramatically -- a nine-fold increase from 270 in 1992 to 2,488 in 1996.
"Health care fraud is the crime of the nineties: fraudulent schemes are ever changing and growing more sophisticated," the Justice report said.

"Unscrupulous persons and companies can be found in every health care profession and industry; fraudulent schemes targeting health care patients, providers and plans have occurred in every part of this country," it added.

Reno told reporters it was hard to quantify how much fraud itself was rising, and how much was more aggressive detection and prosecution. But she said, "We've tried to put additional resources into it, and we will have more resources available to pursue it, to identify it and to take appropriate action."

Among the cases highlighted in the report were a Boston company that sold heart catheters not approved for use in humans, a Minnesota-based kickback scheme, and a San Diego doctor who was performing eye surgery on people who did not need it.
